public_rationale: Part A holds. In March 2026, METR had real maintainers review AI pull requests that passed the SWE-bench coding benchmark. The automated grader scored about 24 points higher than maintainers' merge decisions, and roughly half of the passing pull requests would not have been merged. METR calls the naive reading of the benchmark 'misleading', though it says benchmarks still carry signal. Part C, even read modestly because of 'appear', is contradicted. In January 2026, GPT-5.2 models gave complete, correct solutions to open Erdős math problems, recorded in Terence Tao's database and reported by the Rényi Institute. That is a documented real-world gain outside coding within the 'last few months'. 'Nobody can actually explain' is hyperbole and is not scored.
limitations: METR's sample predates the newest models.
The Erdős results were modest by Tao's own account. A reader could argue they do not show broad extension.
Part C is hedged with 'appear', so the grade depends on how much weight that hedge gets.

our_interpretation: 'It' is LLM capability, mainly AI coding, following 'AI can write code'.

Part A (firm): coding benchmark gains overstate real-world success. Plain reading: benchmark scores are a poor guide to how useful the output is in real work. Tested with studies that compare benchmark results with real-world acceptance.
Part B ('nobody can actually explain') is hyperbole about how well gains are explained. It cannot be measured and is not scored.

Part C ('nor does it appear to extend to any domain outside of coding'): 'appear' hedges it, so it is read modestly. It fails only if, before the post, there was clear and widely reported evidence of real-world gains outside coding, not just higher benchmark scores. Clear results on open problems in mathematics, a domain Karpathy named and Zitron discussed, would count.
Target period: the 'last few months' before the post, taken as December 2025 to the post date of 2026-04-14.
criteria.support_condition: Part A is supported if rigorous studies show coding benchmark scores substantially overstate real-world success. Part C holds if no clear real-world gains outside coding were documented in the period.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Part A is contradicted if studies show benchmark scores track real-world acceptance closely. Part C is contradicted if, in the period, documented and verified real-world results outside coding appeared (for example, open math problems solved by recent models and confirmed by experts).

evidence.excerpt: the automated grader is on average about 24.2 percentage points (standard error: 2.7) higher than the maintainer merge decision. This is strong and statistically significant evidence that the naive interpretation of the benchmark as passing maintainer review is misleading.
evidence.explanation: Real maintainers would reject roughly half of the coding-benchmark passes. That supports Part A: benchmark gains overstate real-world success. METR adds that benchmarks still carry signal, and its newest model tested is Claude Sonnet 4.5.
